strengths: The core idea is compelling and practical: framing black-box model optimization as training a lightweight advisor policy with RL (GRPO) that produces instance-specific natural-language advice, using only API access to the student. This cleanly generalizes static prompt optimization to a reactive, per-instance policy.

Evaluation is unusually broad for this line of work: three specialized reasoning domains (RuleArena Taxes, SWE Agent Efficiency, MTOB) plus three personalization domains, with transfer experiments to frontier models (GPT-5, Gemini 3 Pro) and even across model families (Appendix D.1) and advisor families (Llama, Appendix D.2).

The baselines are treated fairly: GEPA was given matched reward-function access, and the authors reportedly worked with the GEPA authors to verify a fair implementation; the in-context oracle baseline in the personalization experiments is a strong and well-chosen control, and beating it (0.941 vs 0.892 etc.) is a notable result.

The ablations address the right questions: weak vs. strong prompt initialization (Fig. 7), capability retention / catastrophic forgetting (Fig. 8), comparison to direct RL on an open-weight student (Fig. 9, recovering most of the gain), scaling to 100 individuals (Fig. 13), and an honest negative result showing ADVISOR MODELS provide no gains on MATH-500 where knowledge is not the bottleneck (Fig. 10). This 'limits of the method' section is a model of honest limitations discussion.

The cost argument is well-motivated and concrete (training directly on a frontier student would cost thousands of dollars; the modular design avoids this), and qualitative advice examples (Appendix E) support interpretability claims.
Writing is clear and well-organized; figures convey the architecture and results effectively, with 95% confidence intervals reported throughout.
weaknesses: The 'Code available at:' citation is blank, and while training hyperparameters are provided (Table 1), the blank code link plus reliance on a modified SkyRL fork weakens reproducibility for a methods paper whose main artifacts are training pipelines and prompts.

A key control is missing for the transfer claims in Section 4.2: an advisor trained on a cheap student (e.g., GPT-4.1 mini) improving GPT-5 could partly reflect generally useful advice that any optimizer would find. A baseline of a static prompt optimized with the cheap student and then applied to the frontier student (i.e., GEPA trained on GPT-4.1 mini, evaluated on GPT-5) is not reported for the frontier transfers, so the claim that the advisor's dynamic, instance-specific nature drives the frontier gains is not fully isolated.

Baseline coverage is narrow in one direction: all competing methods are static optimizers (GEPA, PAG). Per-instance dynamic baselines such as trained prompt rewriters with SFT, retrieval-based few-shot conditioning, or self-refinement/critic loops are absent, so the strongest available alternative designs for 'dynamic per-instance guidance' are not compared against.

Some evaluation sets are very small (25 test examples for RuleArena Taxes, 49 test issues for SWE Agent Efficiency, 50 for MTOB), and the test sets are subsampled from small source benchmarks, raising concerns about the stability of headline numbers (e.g., 31.2% -> 53.6% on GPT-5 rests on 25 examples); the paper reports CIs but the underlying sample sizes are marginal for the magnitude of claims.

Technical novelty is modest: the method is essentially GRPO applied to a prompt-policy with an API-in-the-loop environment. Related work (PRewrite, DSP, Matryoshka Pilot, BBPO) is well-discussed, but the delta—per-instance advice without expert labels—is an incremental combination rather than a new learning problem or technique, and there is little analysis of why transfer works or when it fails beyond the MATH-500 null result.

Inference-time overhead of the advisor (extra latency, token costs, and the 3-step variant doubling student calls) is acknowledged only in passing (Appendix B.1); no cost-quality tradeoff is quantified, which matters for a paper whose selling point is practicality.

The 'robustness' claim is supported by a single retention experiment (MATH-500 with two advisors, Fig. 8) and one cross-benchmark statement; the evidence is consistent with the claim but thin relative to how prominently robustness features in the contributions.

Several experimental design choices lack justification or ablation: advisor-checkpoint intervals in the multi-turn SWE setting (every 5 steps) are unexamined, and the rationale 'we had access to Gemini credits' for model selection (footnote 1) hints at configuration choices driven by resource access rather than principle.

strengths: The core idea is well-motivated and clearly positioned: reframing prompt optimization for black-box models as RL training of a per-instance advice policy, rather than a static prompt search. This is a natural but underexplored extension relative to PRewrite, BPO, and directional stimulus prompting.

Evaluation breadth is a real strength: three specialized reasoning domains (RuleArena Taxes, SWE Agent Efficiency, MTOB) plus three personalization domains, with transfer across student models, across model families (Appendix D.1), and across advisor families (Llama, Appendix D.2).

Thoughtful ablations that probe the method's boundaries rather than only showcasing wins: weak vs. strong initialization (Sec 4.4.1), capability retention (4.4.2), direct comparison to student-side RL (4.4.3), and an honest negative result on MATH-500 where the method provides no gain (4.4.4).

Effort toward fairness of baselines: GEPA was given an equivalent reward-query budget and the authors verified implementation with GEPA's authors; the in-context oracle baseline is a strong and informative comparison in the personalization domains.
Reasonable reproducibility apparatus: code availability, non-default hyperparameters (Table 1), epoch counts (Table 2), reward functions in Appendix C, and example prompts in Appendix F.
Generally honest limitations discussion, including the admission that gains depend on the domain containing something for the advisor to learn.
weaknesses: Evaluation sets are very small: 25 test examples for RuleArena Taxes, 49 for SWE Agent Efficiency, 50 for MTOB. With single training runs and (apparently) single evaluation passes, several headline claims rest on small-sample differences. The paper does not report variance across training seeds, and GRPO runs at this scale are known to be unstable; the robustness of the gains to seed variance is not established.

The RuleArena Taxes results contain an anomaly the authors cannot explain: GPT-5 scoring 31.2% while GPT-4.1 mini scores 64.8%. The headline '71% improvement' over GPT-5 is computed against a baseline the authors themselves find surprising ('we won't use GPT-5 for our taxes'). This materially weakens the flagship abstract claim, and no decontamination or prompt-sensitivity analysis is offered.

In the personalization domains, the method may be exploiting a reward shortcut: for Review Length and Review Level, the advisor can simply encode the target length/reading level in its advice (as the Appendix E.2 examples show: 'write a 1000-word review'). It is unclear this demonstrates learning 'hidden preferences' in any deeper sense than reward-aware echo of scalar feedback, and the setup (synthetic latent preferences on FSPO) is far from realistic personalization.

Strong dependence on non-stationary closed-source APIs (GPT-4o mini, GPT-4.1 mini, GPT-5, Gemini 2.5/3, Claude) means the numbers are not reproducible in any durable sense, and teacher-of-teacher transfer conclusions may not hold for future model versions.

The 'no degradation on other benchmarks' robustness claim rests on a single cross-domain check (MATH-500 with Math Solutions/Review Length advisors, Figure 8); this is thin support for a general robustness claim in the abstract.

Some baseline comparisons are asymmetric: GEPA is omitted entirely on SWE Agent Efficiency, replaced by a weak hand-written 'efficiency prompt', so the claim that advisor models 'outperform static prompt optimizers' is not tested in the multi-turn domain.

Presentation is sloppy in places: typos ('don't have it's weights', 'the results of the these experiments', 'hhttps' in references, 'Anthropic 2025b' cited as 'Accessed January 18, 2025' for an October release), a reference to 'Appendix 1' instead of Appendix A, and the qualitative 'interpretability' claim about learned advice rests largely on two anecdotal examples.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely problem: how to specialize/optimize frontier models that are only accessible as black-box APIs, where fine-tuning is impossible and static prompts are limited.

The core idea is well-motivated and cleanly framed: re-framing prompting from a static search problem into learning a policy that generates per-instance advice, trained with RL (GRPO) using only environment rewards from the student's outputs — no gradients or labels needed.

Unusually broad and thoughtful empirical evaluation for this type of paper: three specialized reasoning domains (RuleArena Taxes, SWE Agent Efficiency, MTOB) plus three personalization domains, with ablations covering advisor initialization (weak vs. strong), capability retention (MATH-500), comparison against direct RL of the student, scaling to 100 users, cross-family transfer (GPT→Claude), and alternative advisor families (Llama).

The transfer result — advisors trained with low-cost students (GPT-4o mini, Gemini 2.5 Flash) improving frontier students (GPT-5, Gemini 3 Pro) — is the most compelling finding and directly demonstrates the cost-effectiveness claim, supported by the RL-vs-advisor ablation showing most of direct RL's gain can be recovered.

The baseline comparison against GEPA appears fair (equivalent reward-function budget, and the authors explicitly worked with the GEPA authors to verify implementation), and the paper honestly reports negative results (MATH-500 'maxed-out' domain, unexplained GPT-5 underperformance on taxes, untrained advisors hurting performance), which increases credibility.
Hyperparameters, reward functions, prompts, and training details are documented in appendices; qualitative before/after advice examples make the mechanism interpretable.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: RL-trained prompt rewriters/modifiers already exist (PRewrite, Black-Box Prompt Optimization, Matryoshka Pilot, Directional Stimulus Prompting). The main delta — per-instance advice without expert labels, plus transferability — is a useful but largely incremental combination; there is no theoretical or algorithmic contribution beyond applying GRPO to this setup.

Evaluation sets are very small, which undermines the strength of several headline claims: RuleArena uses only 25 test examples (from a pool of 100), SWE Agent Efficiency 49 test issues, MTOB 50. With 40 training epochs on 75 examples (RuleArena), overfitting is a serious concern, and effects like 31.2%→53.6% on GPT-5 rest on a handful of test items; the number of random seeds/replicates for training runs is not reported.

The GEPA baseline is omitted for the SWE domain, so the central claim of outperforming static prompt optimizers is only demonstrated on 2 of 3 reasoning domains, with a weaker ad-hoc 'efficient agent prompt' substitute there.

Reproducibility is limited: results depend on proprietary, versioned APIs (GPT-4.1 mini, GPT-4o mini, GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 3 Pro, Claude, LLM judges for rewards), and model updates will silently invalidate them; the 'Code available at:' link is blank in the manuscript. LLM-judged rewards (GPT-5 mini, GPT-4.1 mini) also introduce reward-hacking/validity risks that are not analyzed.

Several key experimental design choices are confounded: different advisor/student/epoch configurations per domain selected for 'capability/cost considerations', curriculum filtering of the SWE training set (potentially inflating apparent gains by removing hard tasks), and personalization tasks (review length/level) that reduce substantially to memorizing a name→preference mapping, arguably easier than real preference learning.

The robustness claim ('no degradation on other benchmarks') is supported by a single capability-retention experiment, and some claimed general benefits (e.g., 'avoids catastrophic forgetting') are asserted rather than systematically tested. Writing has minor sloppiness ('it's weights', inconsistent appendix references like 'Appendix 1', missing code link).
